title: Subanesthetic doses of ketamine stimulate psychosis in schizophrenia

claims.statement: In the one study read here of ketamine given to people with schizophrenia, 9 inpatients who were actively psychotic but stable, all on a fixed amount of haloperidol for four weeks, received on four separate days over two weeks a blinded injection of salt water and three amounts of ketamine (study conditions: 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, each given over 60 seconds). Twenty minutes later the BPRS total was 33.4 (SD 6.0) after salt water and 38.3 (7.1), 39.3 (5.0) and 45.3 (7.7) after the three amounts, significant at the two larger ones (p = .005 and p = .01), with the psychosis items carrying the change (8.0 to 9.8, 9.3 and 12.3); scores were back at or below their own baseline at 90 and 180 minutes. Seven of the nine people had at least a 50% rise in the psychosis score, one changed by less than 25% and one did not change. What people described often repeated their own illness: at the smallest amount, perceptual distortions, illusions and depersonalisation; at the two larger ones, suspiciousness, delusions, hallucinations and disorganised thinking, with two people whose extensive paranoid delusions returned in part. Four of the nine spontaneously reported symptoms coming back later, at interviews 8 and 24 hours afterwards: two had delusions return about 6 to 8 hours after the injection, lasting several hours and needing no treatment, one reported active dreaming that night, and one reported the same visual hallucinations recurring occasionally over the next several days and declined the second series. These later reports were not rated with any instrument, because they had not been expected, and the paper gives their timing three different ways. The study cannot answer two questions it is often cited for. Whether antipsychotic medication blocks the effect: in the six people retested without haloperidol the BPRS total rose from 37.3 (7.5) to 46.6 (5.9) at the largest amount, reported only as a trend (p = 0.07), no psychosis-score rise was significant, and the comparison between the two conditions rests on at most four paired observations at that amount, with different starting scores. And whether negative symptoms change: the negative-symptom scale named in the methods is never reported, and the sentence stating no change cites a table that holds no negative-symptom measure, while the two people with mainly negative symptoms went in opposite directions (one 50% worse, one 60% better). The order of the four conditions was chosen by non-blind staff for safety rather than randomized, the largest amount was routinely not given first, no blinding check is reported, and there was no comparison group of people without schizophrenia. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Lahti et al. (1995), on haloperidol, 20 minutes after the injection (n = 9, 9, 9 and 7): BPRS total 33.4 (SD 6.0) after salt water, 38.3 (7.1) at 0.1 mg/kg, 39.3 (5.0) at 0.3 mg/kg (p = .005) and 45.3 (7.7) at 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01), against baselines of 34.6, 33.2, 35.2 and 36.9; psychosis subscale 8.0 (3.1), 9.8 (3.3) (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) and 12.3 (2.5) (p = .02), against baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9; at 90 and 180 minutes every value is at or below its own baseline (0.5 mg/kg total 32.3 and 32.3). Seven of nine people had at least a 50% rise in psychosis score. Off haloperidol (n = 6, 5 at the largest amount): total 37.3 (7.5) after salt water and 46.6 (5.9) at 0.5 mg/kg, p = 0.07; no psychosis-subscale rise significant. Four of nine reported symptoms returning 6 to 8 hours later or over the following days, by spontaneous report. No test statistic, confidence interval or effect size is printed anywhere in the paper.
